$comment: All 24 Michigan cities levying an income tax. WIRED into the calculation engine (a later 'go to every state' pass) — see michiganLocalTax() in src/taxes/state.ts, dispatched via certificate.residenceCity/certificate.workCity and read through registry.ts's miCityRuleset(). Rates are flat percentages of compensation; residents are taxed on all earnings, nonresidents only on Michigan-city-source earnings (Uniform City Income Tax Ordinance, MCL 141.601 et seq.).

localTaxScope.rule: CLOSED LIST, DEFAULT ZERO. Only the 24 cities enumerated in `cities` below may levy a local income tax in Michigan. Any Michigan address — any of the state's 83 counties, any township, any city or village NOT in this list — owes $0.00 local income tax, by the same authority (City Income Tax Act, Act 284 of 1964) that limits this power to specific home-rule cities that have individually adopted it. This is what makes 'a random guy in rural Michigan' resolvable: he is not a gap in this dataset, he is the default case the closed list implies.
localTaxScope.confidence: Every source consulted for this file (Treasury's own 'which cities impose an income tax' page, the Grand Rapids consolidated table, independent secondary sources across 3 separate search batches) discusses Michigan local income tax exclusively in terms of this fixed set of cities — none mention county or township income tax, which would be the natural place to if one existed. Two direct attempts to fetch the Act 284 statute text itself (legislature.mi.gov) failed on SSL/navigation errors in an earlier session; MCL 141.631 (the exemptions section specifically) WAS fetched directly 2026-08-12 and is consistent with this closed-list picture, but the section that actually defines WHICH cities/how a city qualifies to levy at all has still not been read directly — this remains corroboration across multiple independent non-statute sources for that specific sub-claim, not a primary-source statute read. Recommend a human confirm that specific section's text directly before this specific claim is relied on for a live customer.
localTaxScope.engineImplication: A correct MI local-tax resolver should look up the work/home city by name against this list; on no match, return $0 local tax with a normal (non-error) result — unlike PA/OH where address resolution can fail and an unresolvable address should error loudly. Michigan's closed-list structure makes 'no match' a legitimate, common, non-error outcome (most of the state's geography), not a symptom of a bad address.
localTaxScope.realExceptionFound: Lansing has '425 tax share agreements' (Michigan's intergovernmental Public Act 425 conditional land transfer mechanism) extending its income tax jurisdiction to specific facilities OUTSIDE its own municipal boundary — confirmed directly on lansingmi.gov this session (GM Delta Township plant + suppliers, Jackson National Life). This is the Michigan equivalent of Ohio's JEDD/JEDZ caveat: the 'closed list of 24 cities, default zero everywhere else' rule is still correct for WHICH ENTITIES can tax, but a person's PHYSICAL WORK ADDRESS being outside all 24 cities' municipal boundaries does not guarantee zero local tax if that address falls inside a 425 agreement zone for one of the 24. Not systematically checked for the other 23 cities this session — Lansing's was found incidentally.

sources.verifiedBy: NEW this session: fetched and read the actual statute text directly. Quoted: 'a deduction of a minimum of $600.00 for each personal and dependency exemption ... on the passage of a further ordinance'. This is the statutory explanation for the pattern seen across all 24 cities: $600 is the ACT 284 FLOOR, not a coincidence or a copied default — a city needs its own ordinance to go higher (Battle Creek/Benton Harbor/Saginaw/Springfield $750, Ionia $700, Hudson/Portland $1,000, Grayling $3,000). This closes localTaxScope's previously-disclosed gap (two earlier SSL/nav failures fetching Act 284 directly) for this specific section at least.

interCityCredit.$comment: NEW this session — the standing rule for a resident of one of these 24 cities who works in (and is taxed by) another. Directly quoted from TWO independent primary sources this session (Albion and Springfield's own pages), both stating the same rule in different words, which is itself evidence this is a uniform, ordinance-level rule rather than a per-city idiosyncrasy.
interCityCredit.rule: A resident of one of the 24 cities who works in and pays tax to another of the 24 cities may claim a credit against their home city's tax, capped at the home city's own nonresident rate (0.5% for the 21 standard cities; the actual nonresident rate for Detroit/Highland Park/Grand Rapids/Saginaw, which differ). Quoted from Albion's own page: 'You may receive credit for taxes paid to another Michigan City not to exceed 1/2%.' Quoted from Springfield's own page: 'Residents working in another taxing city are allowed a credit for income tax paid to that city, i.e. the City of Battle Creek.'
interCityCredit.mechanism: Per Albion's page: 'YOU MUST include page 1 of the other city's income tax return with your [home city] City Income Tax Return in order to receive the credit' — a documentation requirement, not automatic.
interCityCredit.confidence: Two independent primary-source city pages agree on the substance (credit exists, capped at the crediting city's nonresident rate) — stronger than a single citation, but NOT the same as reading Act 284's own statutory text for this specific provision, which was attempted this session via a secondary summary of Chapter 2 rather than a direct primary fetch of the credit section itself.
interCityCredit.detroitException: Form 5469 (already in this file's sources) documents a Detroit-specific version of this same mechanism separately — Detroit residents working in another MI taxing city, and vice versa, per Treasury's own guide.
interCityCredit.knownGap: Not modelled in the engine — no code resolves a taxpayer's home vs. work MI city pair to apply this credit. Not independently confirmed for all 24 cities individually (only 2 of 24 have been checked for this specific provision, though Act 284's uniform-ordinance structure is why 2 agreeing sources is reasonably strong evidence of a shared rule).

knownGaps: RESOLVED: wired into the calculation engine (michiganLocalTax() in src/taxes/state.ts) -- resident and nonresident tax both compute, exemption applies via certificate.allowances (the same count used for state MI_SIT, a disclosed assumption). Inter-city credit is deliberately NOT applied at withholding time -- see the next bullet.

Inter-city credit rule is now documented (interCityCredit above) from 2 independent primary sources, not just Detroit's Form 5469 — but still not individually confirmed for all 24 cities, and not read from Act 284's statute text directly.
Exemption proration for part-year residency varies by city; not modelled.

The 'only cities can levy, everyone else owes zero' rule (localTaxScope) is corroborated across every source consulted but not confirmed against the Act 284 statute text directly — two fetch attempts failed on SSL/nav errors this session (NOTE: MCL 141.631 specifically, the exemptions section, WAS fetched directly 2026-08-12 and confirms the ordinance-by-ordinance structure this rule depends on; the closed-list-of-24 provision itself, believed to be earlier in Act 284, is still unconfirmed by direct statute read).
